title: Class 9 Maths, Chapter 5: Circles, Step by Step
subtitle: For students who find maths hard. One idea holds the chapter together: every radius is the same length, which gives an isosceles triangle and a hidden right triangle. Learn to use each fact first; the proofs come later. Small steps, a picture for every fact, practice with answers. Follows NCERT Ganita Manjari, Grade 9 Part I, Chapter 5 (I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round).

changelog.text: Linked into the Class 9 Maths Part I series: links to all chapters and to the chapters before and after this one.

First version: written for students who find maths hard. Triangle tools first, every fact drawn, using the facts before proving them, practice in levels with answers, and a section for teachers and parents.

topics.label: Start here: the tools you need
topics.desc:
**Goal:** feel sure about the four tools every circle fact uses: angles in a triangle, isosceles triangles, Pythagoras, and drawing a perpendicular bisector.

If geometry has ever felt like a pile of rules, spend time here. Almost every question in this chapter is one of these four tools in disguise.

links.label: Your textbook: NCERT Ganita Manjari, Grade 9 Part I, Chapter 5 (free PDF)
DIKSHA: free NCERT videos and lessons

children.label: How to use this roadmap
children.desc:
- Go in order. Each step is small. On the map the steps go left and right, so press **Checklist view** at the top to see them as a list, in order.
- Click a box to open it. Read the idea, look at the picture, then do **Your turn**.
- **Draw a picture for every question.** In geometry the picture does half the work.
- Write your answer in your notebook **before** you open the answer box.
- Got it wrong? That is fine. Read the answer, then try the next one.
- When a step feels easy, mark it **Done**. Your progress is saved on this device.

**One idea runs through this whole chapter: every radius is the same length.** Draw two radii and you get an isosceles triangle. Draw a radius to a chord and you get a right triangle. Nearly every circle fact comes from that.

children.label: Check yourself (2 minutes)
children.desc: Four quick questions. Write your answers first, then open each box. If you get one wrong, do the step named in the answer.

faq.q: 1. Two angles of a triangle are 50° and 60°. What is the third?
faq.a: **70°**, because the three angles add to 180°. Wrong? Do *Angles in a triangle*.

faq.q: 2. A triangle has two equal sides. The angle between them is 40°. What are the other two angles?
faq.a: **70° each.** 180 − 40 = 140, shared equally. Wrong? Do *Isosceles triangles*.

faq.q: 3. A right triangle has short sides 6 and 8. How long is the long side?
faq.a: **10**, because 36 + 64 = 100 = 10². Wrong? Do *Pythagoras*.

faq.q: 4. What is a perpendicular bisector?
faq.a: A line that cuts a segment **in half** at a **right angle**. Wrong? Do *The perpendicular bisector*.

children.label: Angles in a triangle
children.desc:
- The three angles of a triangle always add to **180°**.
- Angles on a straight line add to **180°**.
- All the way round a point is **360°**.
- **Exterior angle:** if you extend one side, the outside angle equals the two far inside angles added together.

**Worked example:** a triangle has angles 35° and 75°. The third is 180 − 35 − 75 = **70°**. The outside angle next to the 70° is 35 + 75 = **110°**.

faq.q: Your turn: a triangle has angles 90° and 35°. Find the third.

children.label: Isosceles triangles
children.desc:
An **isosceles** triangle has two equal sides. The two angles at the ends of the third side (the **base angles**) are **equal**.

This is the most used fact in the whole chapter, because two radii always make an isosceles triangle.

**Worked example:** the top angle is 40°. The two base angles share 180 − 40 = 140°, so each is **70°**.

**Other way round:** the base angles are 30° each. The top angle is 180 − 30 − 30 = **120°**.

faq.q: Your turn: an isosceles triangle has top angle 70°. Find the base angles.

children.label: Pythagoras (Baudhāyana–Pythagoras theorem)
children.desc:
In a right triangle, the long side (the **hypotenuse**) is opposite the right angle.

**short² + short² = long²**

- Finding the long side: 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100, so the long side is **10**.
- Finding a short side: long 13, short 12. Then 13² − 12² = 169 − 144 = 25, so the other short side is **5**.

Families worth knowing by heart: **3, 4, 5** and **5, 12, 13** and **8, 15, 17**. (6, 8, 10 is just 3, 4, 5 doubled.)

faq.q: Your turn: long side 10, one short side 6. Find the other short side.

children.label: The perpendicular bisector
children.desc:
The **perpendicular bisector** of a segment AB cuts it in half, at a right angle.

**Its special power:** every point on it is the **same distance** from A and from B. This is why it keeps appearing with circles.

**To draw it with a compass:**
- Open the compass to more than half of AB.
- Draw an arc from A, above and below AB.
- Keep the same opening. Draw an arc from B. The arcs cross at two points.
- Join those two points with a ruler.

links.label: Math is Fun: construct a perpendicular bisector

children.label: Congruent triangles, in one minute
children.desc:
Two triangles are **congruent** if they are exact copies. Then **all** their matching sides and angles are equal.

You know they are copies if you can match:
- **SSS:** all three sides
- **SAS:** two sides and the angle between them
- **RHS:** a right angle, the hypotenuse and one side.

You need this mostly for the *why* explanations. For calculation questions, isosceles triangles and Pythagoras do the work.

topics.label: The words for a circle
topics.desc:
**Goal:** know the parts of a circle by name, and see the one big idea: all radii are equal.

Many marks are lost just because a word like *chord* or *arc* is unclear. Fix the words first.

children.label: What a circle is
children.desc:
A **circle** is all the points that are the **same distance** from one point, the **centre**.

- **Radius:** the distance from the centre to the circle. Every radius is the same length.
- **Chord:** a straight line joining two points on the circle.
- **Diameter:** a chord through the centre. It is two radii long, and it is the **longest** chord.
- **Arc:** a piece of the circle itself. A chord cuts the circle into a **minor** (small) arc and a **major** (big) arc.

faq.q: Your turn: a circle has radius 7 cm. How long is the longest chord?
faq.a: The longest chord is the diameter: **14 cm**.

faq.q: Your turn: is a radius a chord?
faq.a: **No.** A chord has **both** ends on the circle. A radius has one end at the centre.

children.label: A circle looks the same every way
children.desc:
- **Turn it** by any angle about the centre and it looks exactly the same. A rolling wheel always looks the same.
- **Fold it** along any diameter and the two halves match exactly. Every diameter is a line of symmetry.

**Try it:** cut out a paper circle. Fold it in half, open it, and fold it in half another way. The two creases cross at the **centre**.

faq.q: Your turn: how many lines of symmetry does a square have? A circle?
faq.a: A square has **4**. A circle has **infinitely many**, one for every diameter.

children.label: The big idea: two radii make an isosceles triangle
children.desc:
Join the ends of any chord to the centre. The two lines are radii, so they are equal.

That gives an **isosceles triangle**, so its two base angles are equal.

**Worked example:** chord AB, centre O, angle AOB = 100°. The base angles share 180 − 100 = 80°, so angle OAB = angle OBA = **40°**.

Whenever you are stuck on a circle question, **draw in the radii** and look for this triangle.

faq.q: Your turn: angle AOB = 60° at the centre. Find angle OAB. What kind of triangle is OAB?
faq.a: Base angles: (180 − 60) ÷ 2 = **60°**. All three angles are 60°, so the triangle is **equilateral**: the chord AB equals the radius.

images.caption: Two radii and a chord: always an isosceles triangle

topics.label: How many circles fit through some points?
topics.desc:
**Goal:** know that through 3 points (not in a line) there is exactly one circle, and find its centre.

This is the section with the compass. Exercise Set 5.1 uses it.

children.label: Through two points: a whole family of circles
children.desc:
A circle through A and B has its centre the same distance from A and B.

So the centre lies on the **perpendicular bisector** of AB. Any point on that line works.

- There are **infinitely many** circles through two points.
- The **smallest** has its centre at the midpoint of AB, so AB is a diameter.
- As the centre moves further from AB, the circles get bigger and flatter.

faq.q: Your turn: A and B are 6 cm apart. What is the smallest radius of a circle through both?
faq.a: The smallest circle has AB as a diameter, so the radius is **3 cm**.

images.caption: Every circle through A and B has its centre on the dashed line

children.label: Through three points: exactly one circle
children.desc:
Take three points A, B, C that are **not** in a straight line.
- The centre is the same distance from A and B, so it is on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
- It is the same distance from B and C, so it is also on the perpendicular bisector of BC.
- Two lines cross at **one** point. That point is the centre, O.

Draw the circle with centre O through A. It also passes through B and C. This is the **circumcircle** of triangle ABC, and O is the **circumcentre**.

If A, B, C **are** in a straight line, the bisectors are parallel and never meet. No circle passes through three points in a line.

links.label: Math is Fun: construct a circle through three points

faq.q: Your turn: draw any triangle. Construct two perpendicular bisectors and draw the circumcircle. Check it passes through all three corners.
faq.a: If it misses a corner by a little, your bisectors are slightly off. Redraw with a sharper pencil. Measure OA, OB, OC: they should be equal.

images.caption: The circumcircle: centre where two perpendicular bisectors cross

children.label: Where does the centre land?
children.desc:
It depends on the biggest angle of the triangle:
- All angles less than 90° (**acute**): the centre is **inside** the triangle.
- One angle exactly 90° (**right**): the centre is the **midpoint of the longest side**.
- One angle more than 90° (**obtuse**): the centre is **outside** the triangle.

faq.q: Your turn: a triangle has angles 30°, 50° and 100°. Is its circumcentre inside or outside?
faq.a: 100° is more than 90°, so it is **outside**.

faq.q: Your turn: a right triangle has sides 6, 8, 10. What is the radius of its circumcircle?
faq.a: The centre is the midpoint of the longest side (10), so the radius is **5**.

images.caption: Acute, right and obtuse triangles in their circumcircles

children.label: Finding the centre of a round plate
children.desc:
You have a round plate and want its centre.
- Draw round it on paper. Draw any two chords that are not parallel.
- Draw the perpendicular bisector of each chord.
- They cross at the **centre**.

It works because the perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the centre. You will see why in the next milestone.

topics.label: Chords and their distance from the centre
topics.desc:
**Goal:** know the chord facts and use the hidden right triangle to find a chord's length, its distance from the centre, or the radius.

This is where most calculation questions come from. Exercise Sets 5.2 to 5.5 use it.

children.label: Equal chords, equal angles
children.desc:
Tie a tight thread between two points on a bicycle wheel. Turn the wheel. The thread moves, but its length stays the same, and so does the angle it makes at the centre.

- **Equal chords make equal angles at the centre.**
- And the other way: **equal angles at the centre give equal chords.**

Why: the two triangles (radius, radius, chord) have all three sides equal, so they are copies (SSS).

faq.q: Your turn: chords AB and CD are equal. Angle AOB = 72°. What is angle COD?
faq.a: **72°.** Equal chords make equal angles at the centre.

children.label: The line from the centre cuts a chord in half
children.desc:
Draw a line from the centre O to the **midpoint** M of a chord. It meets the chord at a **right angle**.

The other way round works too: a line from the centre that is **perpendicular** to a chord cuts it **in half**.

Why: triangle OAB is isosceles (two radii). The line to the midpoint splits it into two copies, so the two angles at M are equal. They add to 180°, so each is 90°.

So the **perpendicular bisector of a chord always passes through the centre.**

faq.q: Your turn: a chord is 10 cm long. The perpendicular from the centre meets it at M. How long is AM?
faq.a: The perpendicular cuts the chord in half: **5 cm**.

children.label: The hidden right triangle
children.desc:
Whenever a question gives you two of these three, you can find the third:
- **r**, the radius
- **d**, the distance from the centre to the chord
- **half the chord**.

They form a right triangle with r as the long side:

**half² + d² = r²**

**Worked example:** radius 5 cm, chord 3 cm from the centre.
- half² + 3² = 5², so half² = 25 − 9 = 16 and **half = 4**.
- The chord is 2 × 4 = **8 cm**.

**The most common mistake:** forgetting to double at the end. The triangle gives you only **half** the chord.

faq.q: Your turn: radius 10 cm, distance 6 cm. Find the chord.
faq.a: half² = 100 − 36 = 64, so half = 8. Chord = **16 cm**.

faq.q: Your turn: radius 25 cm, chord 40 cm. How far is the chord from the centre?
Your turn: a chord of 24 cm is 5 cm from the centre. Find the radius.

images.caption: Radius, distance and half the chord make a right triangle

children.label: Longer chords are closer to the centre
children.desc:
- **Equal chords** are the **same distance** from the centre. (And chords the same distance away are equal.)
- A **longer** chord is **closer** to the centre.
- The longest chord, the diameter, is at distance **0**: it passes through the centre.

You can see it in the right triangle: r stays fixed. If half the chord grows, d must shrink to keep half² + d² = r².

faq.q: Your turn: in a circle of radius 10, chord P is 6 cm from the centre and chord Q is 8 cm from the centre. Which is longer, and by how much?
faq.a: P: half² = 100 − 36 = 64, half 8, chord **16**. Q: half² = 100 − 64 = 36, half 6, chord **12**. P is closer, so it is longer, by **4 cm**.

children.label: Two parallel chords
children.desc:
Draw both right triangles, one for each chord, with the same radius.

**Worked example:** radius 5 cm. Parallel chords of 8 cm and 6 cm. How far apart are they?
- 8 cm chord: half 4, so d = 3 (because 4² + 3² = 5²).
- 6 cm chord: half 3, so d = 4.
- **Same side** of the centre: 4 − 3 = **1 cm** apart.
- **Opposite sides** of the centre: 4 + 3 = **7 cm** apart.

Always draw the picture to see which case you have.

topics.label: Angles made by an arc
topics.desc:
**Goal:** know three angle facts: the centre angle is double, angles from the same arc are equal, and the angle on a diameter is 90°.

These three facts answer most angle questions in this chapter. Exercise Set 5.6 uses them.

children.label: The centre angle is double
children.desc:
Take an arc AB. Join A and B to the centre O, and also to a point D on the **other** part of the circle.

**The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circle:** angle AOB = 2 × angle ADB.

**Worked example:** angle AOB = 100°, so angle ADB = 100 ÷ 2 = **50°**.

How to spot it: both angles must **stand on the same arc**. Trace the arms of each angle and check they end at the same two points.

faq.q: Your turn: the angle at the centre is 130°. Find the angle at the circle on the same arc.
Your turn: the angle at the circle is 35°. Find the angle at the centre on the same arc.

images.caption: Both angles stand on the red arc AB

children.label: Angles from the same arc are equal
children.desc:
Every angle at the circle standing on the same arc is **half** the same centre angle. So they are all **equal**.

In the picture, P, Q and R all see the arc AB at **40°**. Move to anywhere on that part of the circle and you still see 40°.

This is something only a circle does. No other shape has it.

faq.q: Your turn: angle APB = 28° and Q is on the same part of the circle as P. Find angle AQB.
faq.a: Same arc, so **28°**.

images.caption: Points P, Q and R all see arc AB at the same angle

children.label: The angle on a diameter is 90°
children.desc:
If AB is a **diameter**, the angle at the centre is a straight line, 180°.

Half of 180° is **90°**. So any point on the circle sees a diameter at a right angle.

**Worked example:** AB is a diameter and C is on the circle. Angle CAB = 35°. Then angle ACB = 90°, so angle CBA = 180 − 90 − 35 = **55°**.

This gives a quick way to draw a right angle: draw a circle, a diameter, and join both ends to any point on the circle.

faq.q: Your turn: AB is a diameter of length 10. C is on the circle and AC = 6. Find BC.
faq.a: Angle ACB = 90°, so use Pythagoras: BC² = 100 − 36 = 64, so **BC = 8**.

images.caption: Every angle standing on the diameter AB is 90°

children.label: Using radii with arc angles
children.desc:
Many questions mix both ideas: centre angles and isosceles triangles.

**Worked example:** O is the centre, angle AOB = 90°. Find angle ACB (C on the major arc) and angle OAB.
- Angle ACB = 90 ÷ 2 = **45°**.
- Triangle OAB is isosceles: angle OAB = (180 − 90) ÷ 2 = **45°**.

faq.q: Your turn: angle AOB = 120°. Find angle OAB and angle ACB (C on the major arc).

topics.label: Cyclic quadrilaterals
topics.desc:
**Goal:** know that in a 4-sided shape with all corners on a circle, opposite angles add to 180°, and use it.

This is the last big fact in the chapter, and many end-of-chapter questions use it.

children.label: Opposite angles add to 180°
children.desc:
A **cyclic quadrilateral** has all four corners on one circle.

**Its opposite angles add to 180°.** A + C = 180° and B + D = 180°.

Why: angle A and angle C stand on the two arcs that together make the whole circle, 360° at the centre. Each is half of its centre angle, so together they are half of 360°, which is 180°.

**Worked example:** angle A = 85°, so angle C = 180 − 85 = **95°**. Angle B = 100°, so angle D = **80°**.

links.label: Math is Fun: circle theorems (scroll to cyclic quadrilateral)

faq.q: Your turn: in cyclic ABCD, angle B = 70°. Find angle D.
Your turn: careful. Angle A = 120°. Can you find angle B?
faq.a: **No.** B is next to A, not opposite. You can only find **C** = 180 − 120 = **60°**.

images.caption: A cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles add to 180°

children.label: Cyclic quadrilaterals with algebra
children.desc:
**Worked example:** cyclic PQRS has angle P = (3x + 8)° and angle R = (2x + 2)°. Find x.
- P and R are opposite, so they add to 180: (3x + 8) + (2x + 2) = 180.
- 5x + 10 = 180, so 5x = 170 and **x = 34**.
- Angle P = 3 × 34 + 8 = **110°**. Angle R = 2 × 34 + 2 = **70°**.
- Check: 110 + 70 = 180.

faq.q: Your turn: angle A = (x + 20)° and angle C = (2x + 10)° in a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD. Find x and both angles.

children.label: Is this quadrilateral cyclic?
children.desc:
The rule also works backwards: **if a pair of opposite angles adds to 180°, the four corners lie on a circle.**

**Worked example:** a quadrilateral has angles 90°, 85°, 90°, 95° in order. Opposite pairs: 90 + 90 = 180 and 85 + 95 = 180. **Yes, cyclic.**

A rectangle is always cyclic (90 + 90). A parallelogram that is not a rectangle never is.

faq.q: Your turn: a quadrilateral has angles 80°, 110°, 100°, 70° in order. Is it cyclic?
faq.a: Opposite pairs: 80 + 100 = 180, and 110 + 70 = 180. **Yes.**

children.label: The outside angle of a cyclic quadrilateral
children.desc:
Extend one side of a cyclic quadrilateral. The **outside angle** equals the **inside opposite angle**.

Why: the outside angle at C plus angle C makes 180° (a straight line). Angle A plus angle C also makes 180°. So the outside angle equals angle A.

faq.q: Your turn: angle A = 75° in cyclic ABCD. Side DC is extended past C. What is the outside angle at C?
faq.a: It equals the opposite inside angle, A: **75°**.

topics.label: When you're ready: the why, and challenge questions
topics.desc: **For later.** Your textbook explains *why* each fact is true, and the starred end-of-chapter questions ask you to explain too. Come here once you can **use** all the facts above. It is completely fine to skip this milestone the first time through.

children.label: Why the centre angle is double
children.desc:
Join D to the centre O and carry the line on to E on the arc.
- OA = OD (radii), so triangle OAD is isosceles: its two base angles are equal. Call each one x.
- The outside angle AOE of that triangle is x + x = **2x** (exterior angle rule).
- In the same way, on the other side, angle BOE = 2y, where y is angle ODB.
- So angle AOB = 2x + 2y = 2(x + y) = **2 × angle ADB**.

Your textbook also handles the case where the line from D through O misses the arc.

children.label: A hexagon in a circle
children.desc:
A regular hexagon fits in a circle of radius r. Join each corner to the centre: 6 triangles, each with centre angle 360 ÷ 6 = 60°.

Each triangle has two sides r and base angles (180 − 60) ÷ 2 = 60°. All angles are 60°, so it is **equilateral**: each side of the hexagon is **r**.

faq.q: Your turn: how far is each side of the hexagon from the centre, if r = 2?
faq.a: Half a side is 1. d² = 2² − 1² = 3, so **d = √3** (about 1.73).

children.label: Why a cyclic parallelogram must be a rectangle
children.desc:
- In a parallelogram, opposite angles are **equal**: A = C.
- In a cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles **add to 180°**: A + C = 180.
- Both together: A = C = 90°. So every angle is 90°, and it is a **rectangle**.

children.label: The shortest chord through a point
children.desc:
Take a point P inside a circle. Of all chords through P, which is shortest?

The one **perpendicular to OP**. Any other chord through P is closer to the centre (its distance from O is less than OP), and closer chords are longer.

topics.label: For teachers and parents
topics.desc:
**For the adults helping.** Students can skip this milestone.

This chapter states twelve theorems with proofs, which can bury a student who finds maths hard. The roadmap separates **using** the facts (core) from **explaining** them (optional, in the last student milestone). It ties everything to one idea, **all radii are equal**, which produces the isosceles triangle and the chord's right triangle. Those two triangles answer almost every calculation in the exercises.

children.label: How to help a student who is struggling
children.desc:
- **Start with *Check yourself*.** Most trouble here is really trouble with triangle angles, isosceles base angles or Pythagoras.
- **Insist on a drawing** for every question, with the radii drawn in.
- **Teach the hidden right triangle** as a routine: radius, distance, half chord. Then double.
- **For angle facts, trace the arc.** Have the student put a finger on both arms of each angle and check they land on the same two points.
- **Use paper circles.** Folding finds diameters, the centre, and the perpendicular bisector of a chord.
- **Keep proofs separate.** A student who can use all the facts confidently is ready to see why they are true. Not before.

children.label: An 8-period plan, with activities
children.desc:
- **Period 1:** the *Start here* tools: triangle angles, isosceles, Pythagoras, perpendicular bisector.
- **Period 2:** words for a circle; symmetry; the radii-make-isosceles idea. **Activity:** fold paper circles to find the centre.
- **Period 3:** circles through two and three points; constructing the circumcircle; where the centre lands (Exercise Set 5.1). **Activity:** find the centre of a round plate.
- **Period 4:** equal chords; the line from the centre; the hidden right triangle (Exercise Sets 5.2 to 5.4). **Activity:** the thread-on-a-wheel demonstration.
- **Period 5:** chord calculations and longer-is-closer (Exercise Set 5.5). **Activity:** draw chords, measure length and distance, fill a table.
- **Period 6:** the double angle, same arc, semicircle (Exercise Set 5.6). **Activity:** measure angles from several points on one arc.
- **Period 7:** cyclic quadrilaterals, including algebra.
- **Period 8:** mixed practice; exit ticket. The why and challenge questions for those ready.

children.label: Mistakes to watch for
children.desc:
- Calling a radius a chord, or an arc a chord.
- Forgetting to double half the chord at the end.
- Using r as a short side in Pythagoras instead of the long side.
- Halving the centre angle when the two angles stand on **different** arcs.
- Doubling the angle at the circle when the question gives the centre angle (or the reverse).
- Adding **neighbouring** angles of a cyclic quadrilateral to 180° instead of **opposite** ones.
- Thinking every quadrilateral is cyclic.
- Constructing perpendicular bisectors with the compass opening changed between arcs.

children.label: Exit ticket (5 minutes)
children.desc: Five short questions covering the main ideas. The answers are below.

faq.q: 1. Radius 17 cm, chord 8 cm from the centre. How long is the chord?
faq.a: half² = 289 − 64 = 225, half = 15. Chord = **30 cm**.

faq.q: 2. The centre angle on an arc is 140°. What is the angle at the circle on the same arc?
3. AB is a diameter, C is on the circle. What is angle ACB?
4. In cyclic ABCD, angle A = 64°. Find angle C.
5. Where is the circumcentre of a right triangle?
faq.a: At the **midpoint of the longest side** (the hypotenuse).
